transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you for seeing me. Um, well, I guess... it’s been a bit of a process getting here. I'm a software developer, and I work from home mostly, which you'd think would be great, but what finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in today is that I just... I keep getting up when I absolutely shouldn't. 

Like, during our sprint planning meetings at work—which, if you aren't familiar, are these really long, drawn-out sessions where the whole team maps out all our coding tasks for the next two weeks—I just can't seem to stay in my chair. And it's not just work, either. We’ve been on these really important mortgage calls lately with the bank, trying to get all our paperwork sorted out, and it happens there too. 

Even when I know I should stay put because the loan officer is going over critical numbers or my manager is assigning something to me, I just get up. I'll suddenly feel like I desperately need a glass of water right that exact second, or I'll decide I just have to go check something in the other room, like if I left a window open or something completely trivial that could definitely wait. I know I need to be sitting there and being a professional adult, but it's like my body just decides it's time to move and I'm walking away from the desk before I can even stop myself. It’s starting to get really embarrassing, especially on video calls when everyone can see me just wander off.
Do you feel anxious or nervous right before you get up and leave during these meetings or calls?

No, it's not really anxiety. I mean, I guess I get a little stressed about the mortgage stuff in general, because who doesn't, right? But in the actual moment before I stand up, it's not nervousness. It's more like... okay, so even if I'm sitting there and I look totally calm on the webcam, like I'm paying attention and nodding along to whatever the Scrum Master is saying, inside I just feel this intense, building pressure. 

It’s like this physical sensation that I just absolutely have to move, or I need to switch to a different task, or at the very least I need to be doing something with my hands. I keep a whole pile of paperclips and a couple of those squishy stress balls on my desk now, just to have something to fiddle with, but sometimes even that isn't enough. The pressure just builds and builds until I feel like I'm going to literally crawl out of my own skin if I don't stand up right that second. It's not a worried feeling, it's just this overwhelming restlessness that I can't seem to turn off, no matter how much I tell myself to just sit still and be a professional.
Do you feel this intense restlessness when you're not in work or mortgage-related situations?

Um, gosh, you know, I haven't really thought about it outside of those specific situations. I mean... I guess I'm not entirely sure? Because when I'm not working or doing something official like the bank stuff, my time is pretty much my own, right? So if I'm just at home on a Saturday, my husband and I are usually just puttering around the house and I'm always kind of moving anyway. Like, I'll be doing laundry, or organizing the pantry—which is a whole other project I started last month and still haven't finished, but that's neither here nor there—so I'm not really forced to sit in one spot for very long. 

Even if we decide to just relax and watch a movie in the evening, I almost never just sit on the couch the whole time. I'll get up to grab a snack, or I'll bring my laptop into the living room to browse something, or I'll sit on the floor and stretch, or I'll get up to let the dog out. But because it's my own house and my own free time, it just feels normal, you know? It doesn't feel like that intense, trapped pressure because no one is expecting me to be glued to a chair. I'm allowed to move whenever I want. 

So maybe I just don't notice it as much? Or maybe the feeling doesn't even get a chance to build up because I'm already up and doing something else before it can. We don't really do a lot of formal sit-down things in our free time anymore, like long dinners out or anything like that, so I honestly just haven't paid close enough attention to whether the feeling happens when I'm off the clock. It's really just those times when I know I absolutely *have* to sit still and be a professional adult that it becomes this huge, glaring issue for me.
Do you ever feel this intense restlessness when you're in other situations where you're required to sit still for a long time, like in a movie theater or at a restaurant?

Well, now that you mention those specific places, like restaurants and movie theaters... yeah. Yeah, I definitely do. It's funny because my husband and I actually stopped going out to the movies a few years ago. We used to love going to the Alamo Drafthouse, you know, the places where they bring the food right to your seat? But I realized I was just miserable the whole time. Even if it was a movie I really wanted to see, like the new Marvel movie or whatever, I’d be sitting there in the dark, and on the outside I probably looked totally fine, just eating my popcorn and watching the screen. But inside? It's that exact same feeling I get on my work calls. 

It’s this intense, bubbling pressure, like my brain is just screaming at me that I need to move, or I need to check my phone—which you obviously can't do in a theater—or I need to switch to a different task entirely. I would sit there and just furiously shred my napkin under the table, or twist my rings around my fingers until my skin was red, just needing to do *something* with my hands to burn off that energy. And it's the same at nice restaurants, too. If we go somewhere for an anniversary dinner where it's a multi-course thing and you're expected to sit there for two hours... oh my gosh. Even if I'm smiling and having a nice conversation, inside I feel like I'm literally going to crawl out of my skin if I don't get up and walk around. I end up excusing myself to the restroom three or four times just to pace the hallway for a minute. So, yeah, even when I look totally calm and put-together on the outside in those situations, that internal pressure to move is just... it's always there, just waiting to boil over if I'm forced to sit still for too long.
Do you ever find yourself doing things impulsively when you feel this intense restlessness?

Impulsively? Um, I mean... I don't know if I'd say I do things impulsively, really. Like, I don't suddenly stand up in the middle of a crowded restaurant and start doing jumping jacks, you know? It's more just... I have to find a way to let the pressure out, but I'm a forty-year-old woman, I know how to behave in public. I know I can't just bolt out the door of the Alamo Drafthouse halfway through the movie without looking like a crazy person, or without ruining the night for my husband, who really looks forward to those dates. 

So I don't think I act impulsively in the sense of doing wild, unpredictable things. I just... I do the small things I mentioned, like shredding the napkin or pacing the bathroom hallway. And I guess I do those things without really thinking about them beforehand? Like, I don't sit there and plan, "Okay, in five minutes I am going to destroy this paper napkin." I just look down and realize my hands are moving and there's confetti all over my lap. But I don't know if that's what you mean by impulsive. 

I guess I'm just trying to say that even when the restlessness is at its absolute worst, and I feel like I'm vibrating out of my chair, I still try really, really hard to keep it under wraps. I don't just act on whatever urge pops into my head because, well, I have a job to keep and a mortgage to pay and a marriage to maintain, and you can't just go around acting on every single whim when you have those kinds of responsibilities. So, yeah, I'm not really sure if I do things impulsively when the feeling hits. I just try to manage it as best I can without drawing too much attention to myself. Does that make sense? I'm not entirely sure I'm answering your question the right way.
Do you ever feel this intense restlessness when you're doing activities that involve a lot of movement, like hiking or dancing?

Um, well, when I'm doing something that actually involves a lot of movement, like hiking or dancing... no, not really. Because, I mean, if I'm already moving, the pressure doesn't really have a chance to build up, right? Like, my husband and I used to go on these long hikes up in the state park, back before his knee started bothering him, and we'd be out there for three or four hours just walking up these steep trails and scrambling over rocks. And during all of that, I felt great. I felt totally fine, completely normal. Because my body was doing exactly what my brain was telling it to do, which is *move*. 

It's really only when I'm forced to be still that it becomes an issue. Like I was saying before, it's that internal thing. Even when I’m sitting calmly on the outside, and I look like I'm just a normal person paying attention to a meeting or watching a movie, I feel this intense pressure inside. It's like this bubbling, vibrating feeling, like I absolutely need to move, or I need to switch tasks, or I just need to do *something* with my hands before I literally crawl out of my skin. 

But if I'm already hiking, or, gosh, if we're at a wedding and I'm out on the dance floor—which I love doing, by the way, I'm always the first one out there when they play "Shout"—I don't feel that pressure at all. Because I'm already burning off whatever that energy is. It's the sitting still that kills me. The sitting still is what makes my brain start screaming at me to find something else to do, even if it's just shredding a napkin or tapping my foot under the table where no one can see it. But when I'm moving? No, I'm totally fine. I actually feel the most relaxed when I'm physically exhausted from doing something active, if that makes any sense.
Are you usually thinking about something specific when you feel this intense restlessness?

Thinking about something specific? Gosh, um... I don't think so? Not really. It's not like I'm sitting there in a meeting or at a restaurant and fixating on one particular thought that makes me feel restless. It's not anxiety about a project deadline or worrying if I left the stove on, or anything like that. It's much more... physical, I guess? 

Like, my mind might actually be completely engaged in whatever I'm supposed to be doing. I could be listening to my lead developer explain a new architecture for the software we're building, and I might actually find it really interesting! I love problem-solving, that's why I got into coding in the first place. But even if I'm mentally present and following along with the conversation, my body is just... it's doing its own thing. It's like my brain and my body are on two completely different tracks. My brain is saying, "Okay, pay attention, this is important for the Q3 release," but my body is just screaming, "Move! Move! We have been sitting in this ergonomic mesh chair for forty-five minutes and if we don't move right now I am going to explode!"

So, yeah, it's not a specific thought. It's just this overwhelming physical sensation that builds up. And honestly, if I *am* thinking about anything when it happens, I'm usually just thinking about how much I want to move, or how hard I'm trying *not* to move so I don't look unprofessional. I'll be sitting there thinking, "Okay, just keep your hands folded. Don't bounce your leg, it shakes the conference table. Just breathe." It's almost like I have to actively coach myself through sitting still, which takes up so much mental energy. But as far as, like, a specific thought that triggers the restlessness? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. It just sort of happens on its own whenever I'm trapped in one spot for too long.
Do you usually feel any strong emotions, like frustration or irritability, when you experience this intense restlessness?

Frustration or irritability? Um... I don't know if I'd say I feel those emotions specifically *because* of the restlessness. Like, the restlessness itself doesn't make me angry. It's more just... it's just that physical need to move, like I was describing. I don't sit there feeling mad at the world or annoyed with my coworkers just because my body wants to get up and walk around. 

Now, I mean, if I'm stuck in a really long meeting that's going nowhere, and someone keeps asking the same question over and over again, sure, I might get a little frustrated. But that's just normal frustration, right? That's just being a person in a corporate environment where people like to hear themselves talk. I don't think that has anything to do with the physical feeling of needing to move. 

And, you know, sometimes I get frustrated with *myself* because I'm trying so hard to sit still and it's taking up all my focus, and then I realize I've missed the last five minutes of what the project manager was saying. That can be irritating, because I pride myself on being good at my job, and I don't want to be the person who has to ask someone to repeat themselves because I was too busy trying not to bounce my leg. But the feeling of restlessness itself? No, it's not really an emotional thing for me. It's not like a wave of anger washes over me or anything. It's just this intense, physical bubbling feeling that I have to manage. So, yeah, I wouldn't say I feel strong emotions like that when it happens. It's really just the physical sensation.
Do you find that this restlessness happens at any particular time of day?

Time of day? Um, well, let me think about how my schedule usually goes. I do not think it is really tied to the clock, honestly. It is not like I can say, oh, at two in the afternoon every day I get restless. It is much more about the situation I am in and how long I have been expected to just sit there. 

So, for example, it could happen first thing in the morning if I am stuck in a really long sprint planning meeting that is dragging on and on, or it could happen at eight o clock at night when my husband and I are just sitting on the couch trying to watch a movie. It really just goes back to exactly what I was trying to explain earlier. Even when I am sitting there looking completely calm on the outside, like I am just a normal person quietly watching television or listening to a presentation, I feel this intense pressure inside. It is that exact same feeling where I just desperately need to move, or I need to switch tasks, or I have to find something to do with my hands before I literally crawl out of my skin. 

So if we are watching a movie in the evening, which is supposed to be my relaxing time, right? The workday is over, the laptop is closed, we are just hanging out. But if the movie is a little slow, or I am just sitting there without a fidget toy or messing with a puzzle on my phone at the same time, that pressure just starts bubbling up again. I might look perfectly still and attentive to my husband, but internally I am fighting the urge to jump up and go reorganize the pantry or something. And the exact same thing happens at three in the afternoon if I am trapped in a chair for a software architecture review. So yeah, it is definitely not a morning or evening thing, it just depends entirely on whether I am in a situation where I am forced to be physically still for too long, regardless of what time the clock says it is.
Do you have any daily habits or routines that you think might be related to when you feel this restlessness?

Habits or routines? Gosh, um... I don't really think so? I mean, I've been trying to think about this a lot, analyzing my days to see if there's a pattern, because as a developer, you know, I look for patterns. That's what I do. I look for the root cause of a bug. But with this, it's just... no, I haven't noticed any specific daily habits that trigger it. 

I mean, I have my morning routine, right? I get up, I make my coffee—pour-over, usually, because the process of making it gives my hands something to do for a few minutes while the water drips down—and then I log on to check my emails before the daily stand-up meeting. And sometimes I feel restless then, and sometimes I don't. Sometimes I'll go for a run on my lunch break, thinking maybe if I burn off some energy I'll be able to sit through the afternoon strategy sessions better. And, you know, running is great, it's good for my cardiovascular health and all that, but it doesn't seem to stop the restlessness from creeping back in by 2:00 PM if I'm stuck on a Zoom call where I don't have to actively present anything. 

I've even tried changing up my diet, like, cutting out sugar in the afternoons or drinking less caffeine, just to see if maybe it was a blood sugar spike or too much espresso making me feel like I need to jump out of my skin. But honestly? It didn't make a lick of difference. I could be running on zero caffeine and a salad, and if I'm sitting in that ergonomic chair for more than forty-five minutes, my body is still going to start screaming at me to get up. So, yeah, as far as daily habits or routines... I really haven't found anything that connects to it. It just seems to happen whenever it happens, mostly just when I'm trapped sitting still, regardless of what I ate or what my routine was that day.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or activities because of this feeling of restlessness?

Avoiding things? Um... let me think about that for a second. Honestly, no, I don't think I do. I mean, because, well, I can't really afford to, right? 

Like, in my line of work, if there's an all-hands meeting or a really crucial code review that I know is going to take two and a half hours, I can't exactly message my manager and say, "Hey, I'm going to skip this because my legs are going to feel like they need to run a marathon halfway through." I have to be there. I've been at this company for a while, people rely on my input for these projects. So I just go, and I sit there in the conference room, and I deal with that internal bubbling feeling as best as I can. 

And it's the same in my personal life, too. Like I was saying earlier about watching movies with my husband. I don't say, "No, let's not watch the new sci-fi movie tonight" just because I know I'll get that restless feeling by the second act. I love spending time with him, and I want to do normal things, so we still sit down on the couch together. I just might be secretly squirming on the inside, or, you know, finding an excuse to go get a glass of water, or playing with a coaster on the coffee table just to keep my hands busy. 

Or, you know, think about going out to dinner with friends. Sometimes dinners at nice restaurants can drag on for hours, right? You have the appetizers, the main courses, you're waiting forever for the check to finally arrive. I never turn down invitations to those things. I still go. I love my friends. I just know that by the time dessert rolls around, I'm going to be practically vibrating with the need to stand up and walk out the door. But I definitely don't avoid the dinner itself. 

I guess I've just kind of accepted that this feeling is going to happen regardless of where I am, so there's no point in hiding from it or rearranging my whole life around it. I just power through it. Even if it's super uncomfortable and takes a lot of mental energy to just stay in my seat and act normal, I still show up. So, no, I wouldn't say I avoid any situations or activities at all. I just endure them, I guess you could say.
Are you usually thinking about something in particular when you feel the urge to move or leave a situation?

Am I thinking about something in particular? Um... well, it's actually kind of the opposite, I guess? It's not one particular thing, it's more like I'm suddenly thinking about a million things at once. 

Like, okay, let me give you an example from work. I can sit down at my desk with my dual monitors, totally ready to go, and I'll start reviewing a pull request from one of the other developers. And I go into it with really good intentions! I know it's important, I know I need to check the logic before we merge anything into the main branch. But then, after just a few minutes, I'll suddenly realize that I'm just staring at the exact same section of code, like the exact same five lines, and I haven't actually processed a single word of it. 

Because instead of reading the code, I'm sitting there thinking about five completely unrelated things. I'll be wondering if I remembered to take the chicken out of the freezer for dinner, or thinking about how I need to call the plumber about the guest bathroom sink, or debating if I should reorganize my closet by color or by season this weekend. 

And it happens at home, too! My husband and I were looking at some financial stuff recently, and I sat down to read through the mortgage documents. Again, totally good intentions, I really want to know what we're signing and make sure the rates are correct. But five minutes later, I'm staring blankly at the middle of page two, and my brain is off thinking about what kind of potting soil I need to buy for my patio plants or what I'm getting my mom for her birthday. 

So when that physical urge to move hits me, it's usually right around the time my brain has completely derailed like that. It's like my mind just refuses to stay on the one thing I'm supposed to be looking at, it splinters off into all these random, everyday thoughts, and then my body is just like, "Well, we're not actually reading this pull request or this mortgage paperwork anyway, so let's get up and go do one of those five other things." So, yeah, it's never just one specific thought about wanting to leave, it's just this sudden flood of completely unrelated things when I'm trying to focus.
Do you think your mind is completely blank when you feel the urge to move, or are you thinking about something, anything, at that moment?

Oh, gosh, no, definitely not blank! It's—well, it's exactly like I was just saying a second ago, actually. It's the complete opposite of blank. 

Like with the pull requests at work, or those mortgage documents I was just telling you about. I always start out with such good intentions, you know? I sit down, I adjust my chair, I pull the window up on my main monitor, and I tell myself, "Okay, we are going to focus and get through this right now." And I really mean it! I want to get it done. But then... I don't know, maybe three or four minutes go by, and I'll suddenly snap back to reality and realize I'm just staring at the exact same section. Like, my eyes are physically pointed at the same block of code, or the exact same paragraph about escrow and interest rates, but I haven't absorbed a single syllable. 

Because my mind isn't blank at all—it's off thinking about five completely unrelated things at the exact same time! I'll be sitting there supposedly doing a critical code review, but in my head, I'm debating whether I should switch to a different brand of coffee beans, and wondering if it's going to rain later so I should bring my patio cushions inside, and trying to remember the name of that one song that was playing in the grocery store yesterday... it's just a total circus up there. 

It's so frustrating, honestly, because the intention to just sit there and pay attention is one hundred percent there, but the actual execution of it just completely falls apart. I just can't seem to hold my focus on the thing right in front of me. So, yeah, to answer your question, it's definitely not a blank mind. It's a very crowded, noisy brain, and that's usually exactly when the physical restlessness hits its peak and my body decides it just can't sit in that chair for one more second.
Do you ever feel like you're repeating certain thoughts or behaviors over and over when you're feeling restless?

Repeating? Like... doing the exact same thing on a loop? Um, no, I wouldn't say that. I don't think I do that at all, actually. It's not like a broken record or, you know, being stuck in an infinite loop in a piece of code where it just keeps executing the exact same command over and over. It's really the complete opposite of that. 

Because, like I was saying before about all those random thoughts, they're always *different* thoughts. It's never just the same worry playing on repeat. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "I need to call the plumber, I need to call the plumber, I need to call the plumber." It's more like I think about the plumber for three seconds, and then my brain is instantly onto the next completely unrelated thing, like the patio cushions, and then suddenly I'm thinking about a recipe I saw on Pinterest three years ago, and then I'm wondering if I need to update my phone's operating system. It's just a constant, rapid-fire stream of totally new, random things, never the same thing twice. 

And I think it's the exact same way with the physical stuff, too. When I get that restless feeling, like during one of those two-hour all-hands meetings I mentioned, I'm not doing one specific repetitive behavior. I'm not, like, tapping my foot in the exact same rhythm the whole time. I might bounce my left leg for a minute, but then I'll stop and shift all my weight to my right side, and then I'll find myself clicking and unclicking a pen, and then I'll put the pen down and start messing with my watch strap, or picking at the label on my water bottle. It's always shifting to something else. 

Honestly, if it was just one single thought or one single motion repeating over and over, I feel like it might almost be easier to deal with? Like maybe I could just tune it out eventually as background noise if it was predictable. But because my brain is constantly changing channels and throwing brand new things at me, it's impossible to ignore. So, no, definitely no repeating loops. Just a very chaotic, ever-changing mess of thoughts and fidgets, I guess you could say.
Do you ever feel like you're compelled to perform specific rituals or behaviors when you're feeling restless?

Rituals? Um... you mean like having to touch my desk a certain number of times, or having a specific routine I absolutely have to do before I can get out of my chair? No, definitely not. I don't have anything like that. 

It's actually kind of funny you ask that, because I feel like a ritual implies some sort of organization or structure, right? Like a set sequence of events. And my restlessness is the exact opposite of structured. It's just... well, it's whatever happens to be in my immediate blast radius when the antsiness kicks in. 

Like, okay, on Tuesday, we were doing a major deployment to production at work, which means sitting around waiting for the automated testing pipeline to finish. It takes about twenty minutes, and you just have to sit there and watch the screen, waiting for the green checkmarks to appear so you know the build didn't fail. And I was getting so incredibly restless, just crawling out of my skin wanting to get up and walk away from the monitors. But I didn't have a specific ritual I was compelled to do to cope with it. I just sort of... snapped back to reality halfway through the tests and realized I had completely disassembled my favorite clicky pen. Like, the tiny metal spring was rolling around near my keyboard, the ink cartridge was in my left hand, and I was using the empty plastic barrel to tap on my desk mat. 

But I didn't *need* to take the pen apart, you know? It wasn't a compulsion where my brain was telling me the deployment would crash if I didn't dismantle my pen right that second. It was just the closest object to my hands when my body decided it couldn't stay still anymore. If the pen hadn't been sitting there, I probably would have been shredding a Post-it note into tiny strips, or twisting my wedding ring around, or taking my hair out of its ponytail and putting it back up over and over again. 

So, no, there's no rule or specific behavior I feel like I have to follow. It's never a conscious urge to perform a specific action. It's really just this vague, buzzing need to do absolutely *anything* physical to burn off that restless energy, and whatever my hands or feet find first is just what ends up happening. So yeah, definitely no rituals or compulsions at all. Just completely random fidgeting, depending entirely on what's sitting on my desk that day.
Do you ever feel like you must think about something over and over when you're feeling restless?

Like a compulsion? Where I feel like I absolutely have to think about a specific thing? No, no, I don't experience anything like that at all. 

It's really just like I was saying before with the physical fidgeting—there's no rule to it, and there's definitely no feeling of being forced to fixate on one specific thought. If anything, I’d say my problem is the exact opposite! I can't hold onto a single thought if my life depended on it when I get into that restless state. 

I never sit there feeling this intense pressure like, "I have to think about this one specific line of code right now, or I have to run through this specific memory over and over." It’s never a focused obsession. When the restlessness hits, like during those long meetings or when I'm waiting for a script to compile, my brain is just throwing a million completely random, unrelated things at the wall to see what sticks. 

It’s completely involuntary, but not in a way where I feel trapped by one thought. It’s more like being dragged behind a runaway train of just... random trivia and grocery lists and weird memories. I’m never dwelling on one thing. So, no, I don’t feel like I *must* think about anything in particular. It’s just a total free-for-all up there, completely disorganized and always jumping to the next shiny new thought.
Do you ever feel like you're thinking about something over and over when you're feeling restless, and can't stop even if you want to?

Um, no, not exactly. I mean, it’s kind of like what we were just talking about, and I really want to make sure I’m explaining this right, because I feel like there’s a subtle difference here that's really important to how my brain actually works. The problem isn't that I can't stop thinking about *one* specific thing—it's that I can't stop the thinking entirely. 

Like, if I’m sitting in one of our sprint planning meetings... which, by the way, can drag on for literally hours, especially when the project managers start arguing about story points for frontend tickets that don't even involve my team... I get so incredibly restless. Just completely antsy in my chair. And in those moments, I definitely cannot stop my brain from racing, even if I really, really want to just pay attention to the meeting and be a good listener. I'll try so hard to focus, but the thoughts just keep coming. 

But it's never, ever the *same* thought looping over and over. It’s not like a broken while-loop in a script that just keeps printing the exact same error line endlessly until you force quit the process. It’s more like... I don't know, like someone dumped a massive box of random puzzle pieces on the floor and my brain is trying to look at every single one of them at the exact same time. I’ll think about what I’m making for dinner, and then instantly I’m thinking about a weird logic bug in my API code, and then I’m wondering if I remembered to swap the laundry to the dryer before I left the house, and then I'm suddenly trying to remember the name of a character from a book I read ten years ago. 

I can't stop that *flow* of thoughts, no matter how hard I try to just take a deep breath and clear my head. The off switch just absolutely does not work when I'm feeling that restless. But I’m never trapped by one single thought repeating. Honestly, if I could just focus on one thing over and over, even if it was a boring thing, it might actually be kind of a relief compared to the absolute circus that’s usually going on up there. So, yeah, I can't stop the noise, but it's never just one thought repeating itself.
Do you usually feel any strong emotions, such as anxiety, excitement, or irritability, when you experience this intense restlessness?

Let me think about that. Strong emotions... anxiety, excitement, irritability. Honestly? No. It’s actually surprisingly neutral, emotionally speaking. I know a lot of people probably look at me when I’m bouncing my leg a mile a minute under my desk, or when I'm pacing around the breakroom while my coffee brews, and they probably assume, "Wow, she must be really stressed out or anxious about something." But I’m really not! It’s entirely a physical sensation, not an emotional one. 

Like, okay, last Thursday, we had this massive database migration. And it’s a big deal, right? If it goes wrong, we could corrupt client data, which is basically a nightmare scenario. So you’d think I’d be a nervous wreck. And sure, I care about my job and I want it to go well, but when I was sitting there during the migration, tapping my foot so hard my monitors were literally shaking, and flipping my badge lanyard around my finger until it was completely knotted... I wasn't feeling anxiety in my chest. I wasn't scared or worried. My heart wasn't pounding from stress. 

And I wasn't irritable either, even though my coworker, Dave—who sits in the open-plan desk right next to me—kept loudly chewing his almonds. You'd think if I was on edge, that would make me snap, but I wasn't mad at all. I was just... buzzing. It’s literally just this mechanical need to move. Like an engine idling too high, or a car stuck in neutral with someone stepping on the gas. 

There’s just no emotional weight to it. And I’m definitely not excited, either! It’s not like I’m thrilled to be sitting there waiting for a progress bar to load. It’s just this pure, unadulterated physical energy that has nowhere to go. patient.answer:
Repeating? Like... doing the exact same thing on a loop? Um, no, I wouldn't say that. I don't think I do that at all, actually. It's not like a broken record or, you know, being stuck in an infinite loop in a piece of code where it just keeps executing the exact same command over and over. It's really the complete opposite of that. 

Because, like I was saying before about all those random thoughts, they're always *different* thoughts. It's never just the same worry playing on repeat. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "I need to call the plumber, I need to call the plumber, I need to call the plumber." I'm not, like, tapping my foot in the exact same rhythm the whole time. It's always shifting to something else. 

Honestly, if it was just one single thought or one single motion repeating over and over, I feel like it might almost be easier to deal with? Like maybe I could just tune it out eventually as background noise if it was predictable. But because my brain is constantly changing channels and throwing brand new things at me, it's impossible to ignore. So, no, definitely no repeating loops. Just a very chaotic, ever-changing mess of thoughts and fidgets, I guess you could say.

Rituals? Um... you mean like having to touch my desk a certain number of times, or having a specific routine I absolutely have to do before I can get out of my chair? No, definitely not. I don't have anything like that. 

It's actually kind of funny you ask that, because I feel like a ritual implies some sort of organization or structure, right? Like a set sequence of events. And my restlessness is the exact opposite of structured. It's just... well, it's whatever happens to be in my immediate blast radius when the antsiness kicks in. 

Like, okay, on Tuesday, we were doing a major deployment to production at work, which means sitting around waiting for the automated testing pipeline to finish. It takes about twenty minutes, and you just have to sit there and watch the screen, waiting for the green checkmarks to appear so you know the build didn't fail. And I was getting so incredibly restless, just crawling out of my skin wanting to get up and walk away from the monitors. But I didn't have a specific ritual I was compelled to do to cope with it. I just sort of... snapped back to reality halfway through the tests and realized I had completely disassembled my favorite clicky pen. Like, the tiny metal spring was rolling around near my keyboard, the ink cartridge was in my left hand, and I was using the empty plastic barrel to tap on my desk mat. 

But I didn't *need* to take the pen apart, you know? It wasn't a compulsion where my brain was telling me the deployment would crash if I didn't dismantle my pen right that second. It was just the closest object to my hands when my body decided it couldn't stay still anymore. If the pen hadn't been sitting there, I probably would have been shredding a Post-it note into tiny strips, or twisting my wedding ring around, or taking my hair out of its ponytail and putting it back up over and over again. 

So, no, there's no rule or specific behavior I feel like I have to follow. It's never a conscious urge to perform a specific action. It's really just this vague, buzzing need to do absolutely *anything* physical to burn off that restless energy, and whatever my hands or feet find first is just what ends up happening. So yeah, definitely no rituals or compulsions at all. Just completely random fidgeting, depending entirely on what's sitting on my desk that day.
